bibliographic.title: LLM Code Smells: A Taxonomy and Detection Approach
bibliographic.authors: Chenail-Larcher, Zacharie; Mahmoudi, Brahim; Moha, Naouel; Stievenart, Quentin; Avellaneda, Florent
bibliographic.citation_apa: Chenail-Larcher, Z., Mahmoudi, B., Moha, N., Stievenart, Q., & Avellaneda, F. (2026). LLM code smells: A taxonomy and detection approach. arXiv preprint arXiv:2605.22976.

methodology.method_family: taxonomy development; static source code analysis; empirical tool evaluation; software repository mining
methodology.study_design: taxonomy and catalog of nine LLM code smells; development of SpecDetect4LLM static analyzer; empirical evaluation of detection precision/recall and prevalence across open-source projects
methodology.sample_description: 692 open-source software projects integrating LLMs, comprising 171,194 source files
methodology.technology_context: LLM-integrating systems ranging from simple inference to extensive agentic logic; static analysis tool SpecDetect4LLM

eligibility.exclusion_reason: The paper focuses on poor LLM integration coding practices, software quality, and static detection of LLM code smells, not on conversational governance, accountability, compliance, human oversight, or regulated-domain deployment of conversational LLM systems.
eligibility.decision_rationale: Although the study is strongly LLM-specific and methodologically solid for software engineering quality, the provided text addresses taxonomy and detection of code smells in LLM-integrating software systems. It does not discuss conversational AI governance, chatbots/agents as governed socio-technical systems, regulatory compliance, auditability, human supervision, or high-stakes regulated contexts central to the review scope.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: The mismatch with review scope is clear from title, abstract, and introduction; no governance or regulated-domain framing appears in the supplied text.

appraisal.notes: Appraisal reflects only the supplied excerpts. The study appears rigorous for software-quality research, but ethics, limitations, and full analytical detail are not evidenced in the provided text. Transferability to regulated conversational governance is low.

cerqual.explanation: Internal coherence and empirical adequacy for software-quality claims appear strong in the abstract, but relevance to conversational governance in regulated environments is very low based on the provided text.

coding.theme: Software quality and poor coding practices in LLM-integrated systems
coding.subtheme: Taxonomy and static detection of LLM code smells

synthesis.main_claim: Poor LLM integration coding practices degrade software system quality; the authors present a taxonomy of nine LLM code smells, a static detector, and empirical evidence of widespread prevalence and high detection precision.
synthesis.contribution: Consolidated taxonomy/catalog of LLM code smells, SpecDetect4LLM detection tool, and large-scale empirical prevalence and effectiveness results across 692 open-source projects.
synthesis.limitations: Provided text does not state study limitations; scope is open-source software engineering rather than governed conversational deployments in regulated sectors.
synthesis.use_in_review: Exclude as central or supporting evidence for conversational governance in regulated environments; at most peripheral contextual background on technical risks of poor LLM integration in software systems.

evidence.claim: Study presents taxonomy/catalog, static detector, and empirical evaluation.
